Chapter 4: Fairy Tales and the Journey Toward Independence.
Growing up—well, it’s really all about learning to stand on your own two feet, isn’t it? We all start out completely dependent on others, but sooner or later, we have to figure out our own path.
That journey? It’s rarely easy. There’s uncertainty, even fear. And you know what? Fairy tales capture that feeling perfectly, using stories of separation, adventure, and discovering who we really are.
Imagine a child just starting to push for independence—they want to try things alone, even though the world suddenly feels so big and unfamiliar. In fairy tales, this is the heart of the hero’s journey. The main character leaves home behind, faces all kinds of challenges, and eventually comes back transformed.
Take Little Red Riding Hood, for example. On the surface, it’s about a girl visiting her grandmother. But look a little deeper, and it becomes a story about the dangers and temptations that come with stepping out into the world.
The struggles fairy tale heroes face? They’re never just black and white. Maybe they have to outsmart a clever villain, resist a tempting shortcut, or make a tough choice when the stakes are high. In a way, these trials reflect what it’s like to grow up—learning to make your own decisions, coping with disappointment, and finding the courage to keep moving forward when things get tough.
What’s really interesting is how these stories balance the drive for independence with the need for connection. Sure, the hero leaves home, but along the way, help often comes from friends, magical creatures, or unexpected acts of kindness.
The message? It’s okay to stand on your own, but you don’t have to do everything alone.
A lot of kids worry—what if growing up means losing the love and support of their parents? Fairy tales speak to that fear, showing that separation isn’t something to dread—it’s a natural part of life. The road might be rocky, but it leads to discovery and growth.
By the time the child returns home in the story, they’re not the same as when they set out. They come back with new skills, more confidence, and a deeper understanding of themselves and the world.
